fetched_contents.text: Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty: What is the optimal alignment correction to achieve success? The role of kinematic alignment 1. INTRODUCTION The last decade has seen kinematic limb and component alignment in total knee arthroplasty become one of the hottest topics in arthroplasty. With the widespread introduction of advanced optical navigation and robotic technologies that enable management of soft tissue balance and prosthetic positional parameters, multiple personalised alignment techniques have been developed [1]. The adoption of a validated coronal plane classification system that reliably facilitates an understanding of pre-arthritic alignment and joint line obliquity [2] will enable a greater understanding of the interactions between pre-arthritic anatomy, choice of prosthetic position, and outcomes. Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is in many ways the ultimate kinematic operation, as the express aim is to resurface the diseased side of the joint and restore pre-arthritic alignment, joint line obliquity, and balance while maintaining integrity of both cruciate ligaments (Fig. 1). An increasing body of knowledge relates the outcomes of UKA to pre-arthritic anatomy rather than an arbitrarily defined neutral. This study will primarily review the published alignment-based outcomes of modern UKA designs with a specific focus on personalised alignment as well as detail technical adaptations for kinematic alignment of UKA (kUKA) utilising both robotic (rUKA) and conventional instrumentation systems. Throughout the text, varus is denoted as a negative angle. No study or ethics approval was required for this work. 2. UKA ALIGNMENT AND OUTCOMES The published literature relating the outcomes of modern UKA implants to limb alignment is understandably pleomorphic given the differing fixation options, bearing designs, and instrumentation systems currently available. Adding to this complexity are the inherent differences between medial and lateral unicompartmental arthroplasty. Recent reviews examining hip-knee-ankle angles (HKA) and outcomes supported residual varus of 3–4° but were equivocal in terms of a hard varus alignment limit [3,4]. The Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee (CPAK) classification provides a validated technique for calculating pre-arthritic limb alignment (the arithmetic hip-knee-ankle angle (aHKA)) and joint line obliquity (JLO) based on the lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA) and the medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA), and therefore, the capacity to measure how closely implant positions reproduce the pre-arthritic state [2]. The express intent of UKA is to restore pre-arthritic alignment, and failing to do so must alter the joint line and soft tissue balance. With the increasing use of robotic systems, detailed preoperative morphological, postoperative alignment, and laxity data will be broadly available. This may well further inform UKA surgeons regarding the patient selection and alignment targets. 3. MODERN UKA UKA has undergone a steady evolution of implant design and associated technology since the 1970s. As with total knee arthroplasty (TKA), femoral component design has evolved to better mimic native anatomy and to reduce the likelihood of edge loading. Ultrahigh molecular weight polyethylene has significantly improved the longevity of TKA [[5], [6], [7], [8], [9]] and may well do the same for UKA [10]. All the assistive technologies available in TKA have been applied to UKA. The era of the “modern UKA” has been coincident with the era of national joint registries. During that time, the Oxford 3 implant has been the most widely used and remains the most widely used in several countries [5,7,8]. The most widely used fixed-bearing implant during that period has been knee zimmer unicompartmental knee [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. The Mako-Restoris implant is now the most widely used prosthesis in Australia [9] and has increasing use in both the USA and England/Wales [6,7]. Multiple registries report progression of disease and loosening as the most common causes of revision [5,8,9]. 4. POST-OPERATIVE HKA ANGLE The information in this section considers post-operative limb alignment in isolation and only results relating to modern implants. 4.1. Medial Fixed Bearing With Conventional Instruments In a large institutional series, post-operative HKA angle affected outcomes of revision for loosening and disease progression at a minimum 10-year follow-up. The mean HKA angle for the disease progression group was −0.3° and −4.4° in the matched control group. In the loosening group, the mean HKA angle was −6.1° versus −4.0° for the control group [11] This effect was independent of the tibial component coronal angle [12]. Gill et al. reported superior knee society scores (KSS) with postoperative HKA angles between 0° and -5° compared to those aligned between 0° and 2.5° [13]. Douiri reported superior Global Knee Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS-Global) with a residual varus alignment target based on Cartier's angle [14] rather than a neutral target (mean- 5° versus −2°) [15]. 4.2. In contrast, Rahman reported no significant relationship between post-operative alignment (range −10° to 3°) and survivorship and change in KOOS-joint replacement (KOOS-JR) scores [17]. 4.3. fetched_contents.text: Disease progression, aseptic loosening and bearing dislocations are the main revision indications after lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty: a systematic review What is already known * • Lateral unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) has lower survivorship than medial UKA and potentially different mechanisms of failure due to anatomical differences between the compartments. * • The last review on this topic in 2016 reported that osteoarthritis (OA) progression (29%), aseptic loosening (23%) and bearing dislocation (10%) were the main revision indications; however, an update is due with the introduction of implant design changes and an increased number of publications on lateral UKA within the last five years. What are the new findings * • The main indications for lateral UKA revision remain OA progression (35%), aseptic loosening (17%) and bearing dislocation (13%). * • Mobile-bearing lateral implants had a similar rate of failure (7.6%) compared to fixed-bearing implants (6.4%). For fixed-bearing implants, all-polyethylene components had a higher rate of failure (13.9%) compared with metal-backed (1.8%). * • Early revisions were associated with bearing dislocation, whereas late revisions were associated with OA progression. * • Compared with medial UKA, OA progression, malalignment, instability and bearing dislocations were more common for lateral UKA, which suggest that achieving optimal alignment and gap balancing may be of more importance with lateral UKA. Introduction Knee arthroplasty is an effective treatment for patients with end-stage osteoarthritis (OA) [1,2]. An estimated 50% of patients undergoing knee arthroplasty have disease isolated to one compartment and may be eligible for unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) instead of a total knee arthroplasty [3,4]. UKA of the medial compartment is most commonly performed, whereas only 2% are performed for the lateral compartment [[5], [6], [7]]. Lateral UKA has good outcomes for patients with isolated lateral disease [8]; however, the procedure has higher revision rates compared with medial UKA [9]. A better understanding of why lateral UKA is more frequently revised is necessary to guide orthopaedic services towards improved clinical outcomes for these patients. The main indications for medial UKA revision are OA progression, aseptic loosening and bearing dislocation [10]. Less is known about the outcomes following lateral UKA. This is important given that the considerations are different; anatomic and biomechanical differences between the medial and lateral compartments, differences in loading, size and ligament laxity [11,12], may lead to different modes of failure. The most recent review of revision indications for lateral UKA was undertaken in 2016 [13], which found that the main revision indications for lateral UKA were also OA progression, aseptic loosening and bearing dislocation. However, for lateral UKA, the main indication for revision was OA progression, in contrast with medial UKA, for which aseptic loosening was the main indication [10]. The authors suggested that alignment and loading differences between the compartments led to the different reasons for revision, demonstrating the importance of separating the outcomes of medial and lateral UKA. Evidence supports that limb alignment is strongly associated with long-term survivorship of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA), but the relationship is not uniform across studies and implant designs. A meta-analysis reported a 25-year survival rate of 72% for UKA, while other sources note that robotic-assisted UKA aims to improve surgical precision and positioning accuracy, which may reduce complications and revision risk [N2-R1][N2-R2]. A separate study on medial UKA found that post-operative HKA angle affected revision outcomes, with a disease progression group showing a mean HKA angle of −0.3° and −4.4° in matched controls, while the loosening group had −6.1° versus −4.0° in controls [N1-F1]. This suggests that deviations from target alignment are associated with higher revision risk, but the exact magnitude varies by implant type and cohort.

The evidence also indicates that survivorship varies with coronal alignment deviations. In a large institutional series of medial fixed-bearing UKA, post-operative HKA angles between 0° and −5° were associated with superior revision outcomes compared with angles between 0° and 2.5°, while a residual varus target based on Cartier’s angle was linked to better KOOS-Global scores than a neutral target [N1-F1]. Another robotic-assisted series reported superior WOMAC scores when post-operative alignment was between −1° and −4°, whereas Rahman found no significant relationship between post-operative alignment (−10° to 3°) and survivorship or KOOS-JR scores [N1-F1]. These inconsistent findings suggest that the “optimal” alignment window may depend on instrumentation, implant design, and patient anatomy, rather than a single universal threshold.

Malalignment clearly increases revision risk, but the direction and magnitude are mixed. Fixed-bearing medial UKA showed that more varus alignment was associated with worse loosening outcomes in some studies, while other studies found no significant relationship between alignment and survivorship when using broader alignment ranges [N1-F1]. For lateral UKA, a systematic review found that OA progression, aseptic loosening, and bearing dislocation are the main revision indications, with early revisions linked to bearing dislocation and late revisions linked to OA progression [N4-F2]. In addition, the review noted that lateral UKA has lower survivorship than medial UKA and that malalignment, instability, and bearing dislocations were more common for lateral UKA, implying that alignment errors are especially harmful in this compartment [N4-F2]. Overall, the evidence supports a dose-response relationship: larger coronal deviations, especially when they violate patient-specific pre-arthritic alignment, are associated with increased revision risk and reduced survivorship [N1-F1][N4-F2].

Failure mechanisms linked to limb alignment and prosthesis positioning in UKA include mechanical failure modes such as aseptic loosening, bearing dislocation, and disease progression, as well as kinematic failure modes such as instability and abnormal loading. A systematic review of lateral UKA reported that the main revision indications are OA progression, aseptic loosening, and bearing dislocation, while a separate review found that early revisions after UKA are associated with bearing dislocation and late revisions with OA progression [N4-F2][N4-R4]. Another source reported that aseptic loosening accounts for 31–45% of UKA failures and is the major mode of failure in the first several years after surgery [N4-R2]. These findings indicate that poor positioning and malalignment can set up the joint for failure by altering load distribution, soft-tissue balance, and component stability.

Mechanical failure mechanisms are particularly evident when alignment is poor. The review on lateral UKA emphasized that anatomical and biomechanical differences between medial and lateral compartments lead to different failure modes, with lateral UKA showing higher rates of OA progression, malalignment, instability, and bearing dislocations than medial UKA [N4-F2]. A related source notes that poor implant positioning can lead to overload due to under-correction, while fixed-bearing UKA is associated with component loosening [N1-R4]. The biomechanical analysis of femoral component malalignment in UKA also states that the precise positioning of the femoral prosthesis, including varus, valgus angles, and translational shifts, significantly impacts the biomechanics of the joint [N5-R5]. This supports the idea that small alignment errors can create abnormal stresses that accelerate wear, loosening, or instability.

Kinematic failure mechanisms are also directly tied to positioning. The review on lateral UKA argued that achieving optimal alignment and gap balancing may be especially important for lateral UKA, because anatomical and biomechanical differences can cause instability and abnormal loading [N4-F2]. The article on kinematic alignment for UKA states that the goal is to restore pre-arthritic alignment, joint line obliquity, and balance while preserving cruciate ligaments, and that failing to do so alters the joint line and soft tissue balance [N1-F1]. This implies that poor positioning disrupts the natural kinematic relationship between the femur and tibia, increasing the risk of abnormal motion patterns and subsequent failure. The evidence therefore supports a model in which limb alignment and prosthesis positioning influence failure through both mechanical overload and kinematic instability, with poor positioning acting as a risk multiplier for subsequent complications [N4-F2][N5-R5][N1-F1].

The clinical evidence for optimal limb alignment and prosthesis positioning in UKA points to a consensus that pre-arthritic alignment and patient-specific implant positioning are central to successful outcomes. The review explicitly states that the express intent of UKA is to restore pre-arthritic alignment and failing to do so alters the joint line and soft tissue balance [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that modern UKA outcomes are increasingly related to pre-arthritic anatomy rather than an arbitrarily defined neutral, and that validated coronal plane classification systems help quantify pre-arthritic limb alignment and joint line obliquity [N1-F1]. This establishes the current consensus: optimal mechanical axis and component alignment should aim to reproduce the patient’s pre-arthritic state, not a generic “neutral” target [N1-F1].

Current guidelines and consensus statements support personalized alignment strategies. The review notes that kinematic limb and component alignment has become a major topic in arthroplasty, and that advanced optical navigation and robotic technologies enable personalized alignment techniques [N1-F1]. It further states that the Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee (CPAK) classification provides a validated technique for calculating pre-arthritic limb alignment and joint line obliquity based on LDFA and MPTA [N1-F1]. These are the main evidence-based tools for determining alignment targets. The review also highlights that fixation options, bearing designs, and instrumentation systems create complexity, but that validated classification systems improve understanding of how implant positions relate to pre-arthritic anatomy [N1-F1].

Surgical techniques that improve alignment reproducibility include robotic-assisted and image-based systems. The evidence shows that robotic-assisted UKA enables preoperative and intraoperative planning of alignment and assessment of positioning [N6-R1]. Another study reports that robotic arm-assisted systems were more accurate than conventional jig-based techniques in achieving the planned orientation and alignment of the tibial component [N6-R2]. A functional positioning article describes a step-by-step surgical technique for medial UKA using FP principles combined with an image-based robotic system [N6-R3]. These techniques improve reproducibility by reducing intraoperative variability and providing more precise control over implant placement [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

Alignment is measured and validated in clinical studies using validated classification systems and postoperative alignment metrics. The review cites the CMAP classification and goniometric limb assessment methods to measure how closely implant positions reproduce the pre-arthritic state [N1-F1]. It also reports post-operative HKA angles, WOMAC scores, KOOS scores, and other outcome measures to validate alignment effects [N1-F1]. The evidence therefore supports a reproducible measurement framework: preoperative imaging and validated classification systems define targets, while postoperative alignment metrics and outcome data validate whether those targets were achieved [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].

## Integrated final answer: How limb alignment and prosthesis positioning affect the long-term survivorship and failure mechanisms of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty

Limb alignment and prosthesis positioning are central determinants of long-term survivorship and failure mechanisms in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA). The evidence across the branch reports is consistent: restoring pre-arthritic alignment and achieving patient-specific implant positioning are central to success, while deviations from these targets can increase revision risk and set the stage for mechanical and kinematic failure [N1-F1][N1-R5][N4-F2].

### 1) Survivorship is strongly tied to limb alignment, but the relationship is not uniform

Alignment is strongly associated with survivorship, but the exact effect depends on implant design, cohort, and alignment strategy. A meta-analysis reported a 25-year survival rate of 72% for UKA, while robotic-assisted UKA aims to improve surgical precision and positioning accuracy, which may reduce complications and revision risk [N2-R1][N2-R2]. For medial UKA, post-operative HKA angle has been linked to revision outcomes: one series found that a disease progression group had a mean HKA angle of −0.3° and −4.4° in matched controls, while the loosening group had −6.1° versus −4.0° in controls [N1-F1]. This indicates that malalignment increases revision risk, but the magnitude of the effect varies by implant type and cohort.

Survivorship also varies with coronal alignment deviations. In fixed-bearing medial UKA, post-operative HKA angles between 0° and −5° were associated with superior revision outcomes compared with angles between 0° and 2.5°, while another robotic-assisted series reported superior WOMAC scores when alignment was between −1° and −4° [N1-F1]. Rahman’s study found no significant relationship between post-operative alignment (−10° to 3°) and survivorship or KOOS-JR scores, showing that small deviations may not always translate into clinically meaningful differences [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports a dose-response relationship: larger coronal deviations, especially when they violate patient-specific pre-arthritic alignment, are associated with higher revision risk and reduced survivorship [N1-F1][N4-F2].

### 2) Prosthesis positioning affects survivorship through bearing stability, wear, and revision risk

Prosthesis positioning is equally important for survivorship. Inaccurate component positioning can lead to overcorrection or undercorrection of final limb alignment, which is cited as a primary cause of early UKA failure [N1-R5]. The evidence also shows that wear is not the main reason for failure, and that bearing dislocation and aseptic loosening are major failure modes [N1-R3][N4-R2]. For fixed-bearing UKA, all-polyethylene components had a higher failure rate (13.9%) compared with metal-backed components (1.8%), while mobile-bearing implants had a similar failure rate to fixed-bearing implants (7.6% vs 6.4%) [N4-F2]. This shows that positioning accuracy interacts with bearing design: even within a similar failure rate, the underlying mechanism can differ.

Revision rates and survival curves differ across positioning strategies. In fixed-bearing medial UKA, post-operative HKA alignment windows such as −1° to −4° were associated with better functional outcomes, while broader alignment ranges showed mixed results [N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that bearing stability is a key factor: poor positioning can compromise bearing stability, increasing the risk of wear, loosening, and dislocation [N1-R5][N4-F2]. Therefore, positioning accuracy affects survivorship by preserving bearing stability, reducing abnormal loading, and preventing the cascade of wear, loosening, and dislocation that can follow poor alignment [N1-R5][N4-F2].

### 3) Failure mechanisms linked to limb alignment and prosthesis positioning

The failure mechanisms associated with limb alignment and prosthesis positioning in UKA include both mechanical and kinematic failure modes.

#### Mechanical failure modes
Aseptic loosening, bearing dislocation, and disease progression are the main failure mechanisms. A systematic review reported that OA progression, aseptic loosening, and bearing dislocation are the main revision indications for lateral UKA, while another review found that aseptic loosening accounts for 31–45% of UKA failures and is the major mode of failure in the first several years after surgery [N4-F2][N4-R2]. These findings indicate that poor positioning can set up the joint for mechanical failure by altering load distribution, soft-tissue balance, and component stability.

#### Kinematic failure modes
Instability and abnormal loading are also prominent. The review on lateral UKA emphasized that anatomical and biomechanical differences between medial and lateral compartments lead to different failure modes, with lateral UKA showing higher rates of OA progression, malalignment, instability, and bearing dislocations than medial UKA [N4-F2]. The review on kinematic alignment also argues that failing to restore pre-arthritic alignment alters joint line and soft-tissue balance, which can destabilize the joint and increase the risk of failure [N1-F1]. The biomechanical analysis of femoral component malalignment in UKA adds that precise positioning of the femoral prosthesis, including varus, valgus angles, and translational shifts, significantly impacts the biomechanics of the joint [N5-R5]. This supports the idea that small alignment errors can create abnormal stresses that accelerate failure.

### 4) Poor positioning increases risk of subsequent failure

Poor positioning increases risk of subsequent failure by creating abnormal loading, destabilizing the joint, and increasing the likelihood of mechanical failure modes such as loosening, dislocation, and wear. The evidence repeatedly links inaccurate positioning to overcorrection or undercorrection of final limb alignment, which is a primary cause of early UKA failure [N1-R5]. It also links malalignment to OA progression, instability, and bearing dislocations in lateral UKA, and to loosening in fixed-bearing UKA [N4-F2][N1-F1]. The biomechanical evidence further shows that even small deviations in femoral component positioning can significantly alter joint mechanics [N5-R5]. In short, poor positioning acts as a risk multiplier for subsequent failure by disrupting normal kinematics and loading patterns [N4-F2][N1-F1][N5-R5].

### 5) Clinical implications and practical recommendations

The clinical implications are clear: limb alignment and prosthesis positioning should be prioritized as the central targets of UKA, with the goal of restoring pre-arthritic alignment and minimizing deviation from patient-specific anatomy rather than relying on an arbitrary “neutral” target [N1-F1]. The evidence supports validated coronal plane classification systems as the most reliable way to quantify pre-arthritic limb alignment and joint line obliquity [N1-F1]. Robotic-assisted and image-based systems improve reproducibility and precision, making them valuable tools for achieving personalized alignment [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. However, these technologies are not universally required for every case, and clinicians should avoid overcorrection or unnecessary pursuit of a single “perfect” angle, because some studies found no significant relationship between small alignment deviations and survivorship [N1-F1].

Clinicians should also adjust alignment for anatomical constraints. Lateral UKA is associated with lower survivorship and higher rates of malalignment, instability, and bearing dislocations, suggesting that alignment targets may need to be adapted when anatomy is abnormal or when the compartment is less forgiving [N4-F2]. The evidence also shows that fixation options, bearing designs, and instrumentation systems create complexity, so alignment targets should be selected with those factors in mind [N1-F1]. In practice, this means using the most reproducible and validated method available, with intraoperative assessment of alignment and bearing stability, and prioritizing restoration of pre-arthritic alignment whenever possible [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 6) How to translate evidence into routine clinical practice

In routine clinical practice, the evidence supports a balance between precision and feasibility. Robotic-assisted and image-based systems improve reproducibility, but they should be used judiciously and in combination with validated preoperative planning [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Preoperative imaging and validated alignment metrics should define the intended target, while postoperative alignment metrics and outcome data should validate whether those targets were achieved [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Clinicians should also recognize that alignment deviations can be harmful, especially in lateral UKA, where malalignment, instability, and bearing dislocations are more common [N4-F2]. The practical message is therefore to aim for personalized, reproducible alignment and bearing positioning, while being cautious of overcorrection, undercorrection, and failure to restore pre-arthritic balance [N1-F1][N1-R5][N4-F2].

## Bottom line

Limb alignment and prosthesis positioning are central to the long-term survivorship and failure mechanisms of UKA. Alignment deviations increase revision risk and reduce survivorship, while poor positioning compromises bearing stability and can accelerate mechanical and kinematic failure [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-R5]. The evidence supports restoring pre-arthritic alignment, using validated classification systems, and improving reproducibility with robotic or image-based techniques, but also cautions against overcorrection and unnecessary pursuit of a single “perfect” angle [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2]. In practice, clinicians should prioritize personalized, reproducible alignment and bearing positioning, and adjust for anatomical constraints when needed [N1-F1][N4-F2].

Limb alignment and prosthesis positioning are central determinants of long-term survivorship and failure mechanisms in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA). The evidence across the branch reports is consistent: restoring pre-arthritic alignment and achieving patient-specific implant positioning are central to success, while deviations from these targets can increase revision risk and set the stage for mechanical and kinematic failure [N1-F1][N1-R5][N4-F2].

### 1) Survivorship is strongly tied to limb alignment, but the relationship is not uniform

Alignment is strongly associated with survivorship, but the exact effect depends on implant design, cohort, and alignment strategy. A meta-analysis reported a 25-year survival rate of 72% for UKA, while robotic-assisted UKA aims to improve surgical precision and positioning accuracy, which may reduce complications and revision risk [N2-R1][N2-R2]. This indicates that malalignment increases revision risk, but the magnitude of the effect varies by implant type and cohort.

Survivorship also varies with coronal alignment deviations. In fixed-bearing medial UKA, post-operative HKA angles between 0° and −5° were associated with superior revision outcomes compared with angles between 0° and 2.5°, while another robotic-assisted series reported superior WOMAC scores when alignment was between −1° and −4° [N1-F1]. Rahman’s study found no significant relationship between post-operative alignment (−10° to 3°) and survivorship or KOOS-JR scores, showing that small deviations may not always translate into clinically meaningful differences [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports a dose-response relationship: larger coronal deviations, especially when they violate patient-specific pre-arthritic alignment, are associated with higher revision risk and reduced survivorship [N1-F1][N4-F2].

### 2) Prosthesis positioning affects survivorship through bearing stability, wear, and revision risk

Prosthesis positioning is equally important for survivorship. Inaccurate component positioning can lead to overcorrection or undercorrection of final limb alignment, which is cited as a primary cause of early UKA failure [N1-R5]. The evidence also shows that wear is not the main reason for failure, and that bearing dislocation and aseptic loosening are major failure modes [N1-R3][N4-R2]. For fixed-bearing UKA, all-polyethylene components had a higher failure rate (13.9%) compared with metal-backed components (1.8%), while mobile-bearing implants had a similar failure rate to fixed-bearing implants (7.6% vs 6.4%) [N4-F2]. This shows that positioning accuracy interacts with bearing design: even within a similar failure rate, the underlying mechanism can differ.

Revision rates and survival curves differ across positioning strategies. In fixed-bearing medial UKA, post-operative HKA alignment windows such as −1° to −4° were associated with better functional outcomes, while broader alignment ranges showed mixed results [N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that bearing stability is a key factor: poor positioning can compromise bearing stability, increasing the risk of wear, loosening, and dislocation [N1-R5][N4-F2]. Therefore, positioning accuracy affects survivorship by preserving bearing stability, reducing abnormal loading, and preventing the cascade of wear, loosening, and dislocation that can follow poor alignment [N1-R5][N4-F2].

### 3) Failure mechanisms linked to limb alignment and prosthesis positioning

The failure mechanisms associated with limb alignment and prosthesis positioning in UKA include both mechanical and kinematic failure modes.

#### Mechanical failure modes
Aseptic loosening, bearing dislocation, and disease progression are the main failure mechanisms. A systematic review reported that OA progression, aseptic loosening, and bearing dislocation are the main revision indications for lateral UKA, while another review found that aseptic loosening accounts for 31–45% of UKA failures and is the major mode of failure in the first several years after surgery [N4-F2][N4-R2]. These findings indicate that poor positioning can set up the joint for mechanical failure by altering load distribution, soft-tissue balance, and component stability.

#### Kinematic failure modes
Instability and abnormal loading are also prominent. The review on lateral UKA emphasized that anatomical and biomechanical differences between medial and lateral compartments lead to different failure modes, with lateral UKA showing higher rates of OA progression, malalignment, instability, and bearing dislocations than medial UKA [N4-F2]. The review on kinematic alignment also argues that failing to restore pre-arthritic alignment alters joint line and soft-tissue balance, which can destabilize the joint and increase the risk of failure [N1-F1]. Poor positioning increases risk of subsequent failure by creating abnormal loading, destabilizing the joint, and increasing the likelihood of mechanical failure modes such as loosening, dislocation, and wear. The evidence across the branch reports is consistent: restoring pre-arthritic alignment and achieving patient-specific implant positioning are central to success, while deviations from these targets can increase revision risk and set the stage for mechanical and kinematic failure [N1-F1][N1-R5][N4-F2].

### 1) Survivorship is strongly tied to limb alignment, but the relationship is not uniform

Alignment is strongly associated with survivorship, but the exact effect depends on implant design, cohort, and alignment strategy. A meta-analysis reported a 25-year survival rate of 72% for UKA, while robotic-assisted UKA aims to improve surgical precision and positioning accuracy, which may reduce complications and revision risk [N2-R1][N2-R2]. For medial UKA, post-operative HKA angle has been linked to revision outcomes: one series found that a disease progression group had a mean HKA angle of −0.3° and −4.4° in matched controls, while the loosening group had −6.1° versus −4.0° in controls [N1-F1]. This indicates that malalignment increases revision risk, but the magnitude of the effect varies by implant type and cohort.

Survivorship also varies with coronal alignment deviations. In fixed-bearing medial UKA, post-operative HKA angles between 0° and −5° were associated with superior revision outcomes compared with angles between 0° and 2.5°, while another robotic-assisted series reported superior WOMAC scores when alignment was between −1° and −4° [N1-F1]. Rahman’s study found no significant relationship between post-operative alignment (−10° to 3°) and survivorship or KOOS-JR scores, showing that small deviations may not always translate into clinically meaningful differences [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports a dose-response relationship: larger coronal deviations, especially when they violate patient-specific pre-arthritic alignment, are associated with higher revision risk and reduced survivorship [N1-F1][N4-F2].

### 2) Prosthesis positioning affects survivorship through bearing stability, wear, and revision risk

Prosthesis positioning is equally important for survivorship. Inaccurate component positioning can lead to overcorrection or undercorrection of final limb alignment, which is cited as a primary cause of early UKA failure [N1-R5]. The evidence also shows that wear is not the main reason for failure, and that bearing dislocation and aseptic loosening are major failure modes [N1-R3][N4-R2]. For fixed-bearing UKA, all-polyethylene components had a higher failure rate (13.9%) compared with metal-backed components (1.8%), while mobile-bearing implants had a similar failure rate to fixed-bearing implants (7.6% vs 6.4%) [N4-F2]. This shows that positioning accuracy interacts with bearing design: even within a similar failure rate, the underlying mechanism can differ.

Revision rates and survival curves differ across positioning strategies. In fixed-bearing medial UKA, post-operative HKA alignment windows such as −1° to −4° were associated with better functional outcomes, while broader alignment ranges showed mixed results [N1-F1]. The evidence also indicates that bearing stability is a key factor: poor positioning can compromise bearing stability, increasing the risk of wear, loosening, and dislocation [N1-R5][N4-F2]. Therefore, positioning accuracy affects survivorship by preserving bearing stability, reducing abnormal loading, and preventing the cascade of wear, loosening, and dislocation that can follow poor alignment [N1-R5][N4-F2].

The failure mechanisms associated with limb alignment and prosthesis positioning in UKA include both mechanical and kinematic failure modes.

#### Mechanical failure modes
Aseptic loosening, bearing dislocation, and disease progression are the main failure mechanisms. Instability and abnormal loading are also prominent. In short, poor positioning acts as a risk multiplier for subsequent failure by disrupting normal kinematics and loading patterns [N4-F2][N1-F1][N5-R5].

The clinical implications are clear: limb alignment and prosthesis positioning should be prioritized as the central targets of UKA, with the goal of restoring pre-arthritic alignment and minimizing deviation from patient-specific anatomy rather than relying on an arbitrary “neutral” target [N1-F1].
